newsitem.title: USA: US Stockpile rules out mercury sales in FY97.
newsitem.headline: US Stockpile rules out mercury sales in FY97.

text.p: The U.S. Defense National Stockpile Center said resuming sales of mercury from the government's hoard of surplus material was effectively ruled out in the current fiscal year which ends September 30.
"I don't believe we will be selling mercury in the next few months," Robert O'Brien, deputy stockpile administrator said.
The stockpile wants to sell mercury but met opposition from the Environmental Protection Agency and voluntarily suspended sales in 1994.
O'Brien said an independent consultant has been hired to look at the environmental and economic impact of sales of stockpiled mercury and will report back within two months.
"The commodity is viable and commercial and we have 130,000 flasks of material and would only too much like to offer it to the market place," O'Brien told Metal Bulletin's Minor Metals Seminar.
A flask of mercury weighs 76 pounds and is the standard unit of sale for the heavy metal.
Once the independent study is completed, a lengthy consultation process will begin, including meetings with the mercury industry and traders which would take several months, O'Brien said.
The stockpile receives many letters, largely against resumption of selling mercury, a poisonous metal, O'Brien said.
O'Brien said the EPA was itself divided on the issue of mercury sales.

Bruce Lawrence, President of Bethlehem Apparatus, a recycler of mercury in the U.S., said in his presentation at the same seminar that his company sometimes has to go to Europe to buy mercury despite the existence of a large domestic stockpiles, including 50,000 flasks of secondary mercury held by the U.S. Energy Dept.
"We have all this mercury here but I have to go to Europe to buy mercury. That does not make sense to me and others," Lawrence said.
